data/auth:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Managed end-user auth is live.
> Auth is **opt-in** and disabled by default.
> Enable it for a sandbox or deployment and MIOSA provisions the auth schema in the linked managed database.
> The runtime receives `AUTH_URL`, `AUTH_JWT_SECRET`, and `AUTH_DATABASE_URL`.

## Opt-in model

Auth is disabled by default.
A sandbox or deployment has no managed signup surface until you enable it.
This prevents accidental exposure of authentication endpoints.

**Enable via API:**
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/project-auth/enable \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "resource_type": "sandbox",
    "resource_id": "'"$SANDBOX_ID"'",
    "config": {
      "signup_enabled": true,
      "email_confirm_required": false,
      "token_expiry_sec": 3600
    }
  }'
```

If the linked database is still provisioning, the endpoint returns `202` with `state: "pending"`.
Poll the status endpoint until auth is active:

```bash
curl \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/project-auth/status?resource_type=sandbox&resource_id=$SANDBOX_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

For running sandboxes, MIOSA attempts to synchronize the auth variables into the current runtime.
Deployment changes follow the deployment environment and release lifecycle.

---

Auth is the opt-in managed-auth experience.
When enabled, MIOSA provisions auth tables in the linked database.
The app receives:
```bash

AUTH_URL=https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/app-auth/sandbox/<sandbox-id>
AUTH_JWT_SECRET=<random 64-char hex>
AUTH_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...
```

The generated app uses them like this:
```typescript
// Sign up a new end user
const res = await fetch(`${process.env.AUTH_URL}/signup`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
})
const { access_token, user } = await res.json()

// Verify a JWT in the app's own API
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken"
const claims = jwt.verify(token, process.env.AUTH_JWT_SECRET!)
const userId = claims.sub
```

That's the agent-on-day-zero experience: agent writes a signup flow on day zero, never has to ask the user to configure auth.

## What's offered

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Email + password signup / login | Available |
| JWT access tokens | Available |
| Token verify | Available |
| Email verification | Available (requires email delivery configured) |
| Password reset | Available (requires email delivery configured) |
| Organization SSO (SAML) | Available (configure per organization; enforce SSO for members) |

Not offered today: refresh tokens, magic links, OAuth providers such as Google and GitHub, MFA and TOTP, and passkeys and WebAuthn. Plan for the flows above, and hold your own session lifetime outside the access token. See [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations) for the full list.

## Endpoints
`AUTH_URL` already points at the resource-specific base (`.../app-auth/<type>/<id>`).
Append the action path:
```http
POST   {AUTH_URL}/signup                   create an end-user account → JWT
POST   {AUTH_URL}/login                    authenticate → JWT
POST   {AUTH_URL}/verify                   verify a JWT, returns the claims
POST   {AUTH_URL}/password-reset           request a reset link (sends email*)
POST   {AUTH_URL}/password-reset/confirm   complete the reset with the token
POST   {AUTH_URL}/email/confirm            confirm an email with the token
```
\* `/password-reset` and `/email/confirm` only send mail once email delivery is
configured; see below. The endpoints succeed regardless; the email is the part
that needs setup.

## Configuring email delivery

Password reset and email verification generate the token and call the send, but
the email itself only goes out once an email provider is wired up. **Until then,
those endpoints return success but no email is sent** (the platform logs
`email_not_configured` and skips it; it never crashes the auth flow).

MIOSA currently sends built-in auth email through an operator-managed delivery provider.
See [Transactional Email](/docs/data/email) for the verification checklist and white-label sender boundaries.
There is no self-service per-resource sender credential in the current public contract.

> Today email sends from a single platform-wide address. Per-project and
> custom-domain senders, so each white-label brand's emails come from its own
> domain, are not offered today.

## End users are not MIOSA users

Important distinction:

- **MIOSA platform user** = the developer / platform builder. Authenticates with `msk_*` API keys or JWT sessions issued by MIOSA. Has access to the MIOSA dashboard.
- **End user of a generated app** = the visitor to an app YOUR PLATFORM built (e.g. a customer logging into an app your platform built). Authenticates against the per-project `AUTH_URL`. Has no MIOSA account.

These are completely separate auth systems. The same email can be a MIOSA platform user AND an end user of someone's app; they're different records, with different password hashes.

## Per-project isolation

Each enabled resource receives an isolated auth scope and JWT secret.
A token issued for one resource cannot authenticate against a different resource.

This makes the "end user signs up to a generated app" pattern safe even when the same MIOSA tenant hosts thousands of independent end-user apps.

## Row-level security (Postgres pattern)

When combined with managed [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres), the auth JWT carries the user ID (`sub` claim). Your runtime code uses it for row-level filtering:
```typescript
const claims = jwt.verify(token, process.env.AUTH_JWT_SECRET!)

const orders = await pool.query(
  "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1",
  [claims.sub]
)
```

Or use Postgres RLS policies if your Postgres has them enabled:
```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY order_owner ON orders
  USING (customer_id = current_setting('jwt.claims.sub')::uuid);
```

## Bring your own auth?

Yes. Skip the managed auth, set your own `AUTH_URL` and `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` to point at Clerk / Auth0 / your own service. MIOSA's runtime injects whatever you set.

## Python SDK

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# Get current managed-auth status and config
status = miosa.project_auth.status(
    resource_type="sandbox",
    resource_id=sandbox_id,
)
print(status)  # {"enabled": false, ...}

# Enable project auth (with optional config kwargs)
miosa.project_auth.enable(
    resource_type="sandbox",
    resource_id=sandbox_id,
    signup_enabled=True,
)

# Update config after enabling
miosa.project_auth.update(
    resource_type="sandbox",
    resource_id=sandbox_id,
    signup_enabled=False,
)

# Disable when no longer needed
miosa.project_auth.disable(
    resource_type="sandbox",
    resource_id=sandbox_id,
)
```

## See also

- [Overview](/docs/data/overview)  -  the broader data plane
- [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres)  -  pairs naturally with auth for RLS
- [Platform / Browser Tokens](/docs/platform/browser-tokens)  -  for MIOSA-level browser access; distinct from your app's end-user auth
data/email:
MIOSA uses transactional email for platform notifications and for per-project
end-user auth flows such as password reset and email confirmation.

This page separates three different email patterns:

| Pattern | Who owns it | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **MIOSA-managed auth email** | MIOSA/operator | Password reset, email confirmation, security notices |
| **App-owned transactional email** | The generated app/customer | Receipts, booking confirmations, workflow notices |
| **Enterprise/private sender setup** | MIOSA + customer/operator | White-label sender domains, private SMTP, compliance-bound delivery |

> **Note: Current production model**
>
> The live MIOSA-managed auth path uses Resend today. That does not mean Resend is
> the only email provider a customer app can use. It means the built-in Project
> Auth sender currently reads the platform Resend configuration.

## What email covers

| Flow | Uses this config? | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Project Auth password reset | Yes | Sends a reset link for an end user of a generated app. |
| Project Auth email confirmation | Yes | Sends a confirmation link after signup when email verification is enabled. |
| Platform admin/user notifications | Yes | Uses the same Resend API key, with platform mailer settings. |
| Customer application transactional email | No | Wire the app to its own provider integration or runtime secret. |
| Customer marketing/campaign email | No | Usually belongs in the customer app or marketing stack, not MIOSA auth. |

## MIOSA-managed auth email

MIOSA operators configure the shared delivery provider and sender identity for the built-in Auth-as-a-Service product.
Customer applications do not receive or manage the platform delivery credential.

If platform delivery is unavailable, auth can still generate reset or confirmation tokens, but the corresponding email is not delivered.
Do not treat a successful password-reset response as proof that a message reached the provider or inbox.

## Other provider options

For application-level email, the generated app can use whichever provider the
customer chooses. Common patterns:

| Provider model | Good for | How it should be wired |
|---|---|---|
| **Resend** | Developer-friendly transactional email | Store the app's `RESEND_API_KEY` as a project/runtime secret and call Resend from app code. |
| **Postmark** | High-deliverability transactional email | Store a server token as a secret; app owns templates and sender verification. |
| **SendGrid** | Larger enterprise email programs | Store API key as a secret or enterprise integration; app owns templates/categories. |
| **Mailgun** | Domain-heavy transactional email | Store API key/domain as secrets; app owns routing and logs. |
| **SMTP relay** | Enterprise/private mail infrastructure | Store SMTP host/user/password as secrets or configure a private deployment path. |
| **Customer-owned service** | Regulated or on-prem environments | Scope network path, credentials, audit, and data handling in the enterprise deployment. |

The important rule: app-owned providers are not the same as MIOSA's built-in
auth mailer. App email belongs to the application runtime; MIOSA auth email
belongs to the platform control plane.

## Platform mailer and notifications

The platform mailer and Auth-as-a-Service use operator-managed delivery configuration.
Platform notification and app-auth sender policies can differ even when they use the same provider.

Do not treat a successful password-reset API response as proof an email was
sent. Check provider configuration, logs, and the provider event dashboard.

## Verification checklist

After configuring the env vars:

1. Enable Project Auth for a fresh project or sandbox.
2. Create a test end user through `{AUTH_URL}/signup`.
3. Call `{AUTH_URL}/password-reset` for that email.
4. Confirm the backend does not log `email_not_configured`.
5. Confirm the configured provider accepts the message.
6. Confirm the reset link reaches the inbox and `{AUTH_URL}/password-reset/confirm` accepts the token.

## White-label and enterprise senders

Today the built-in auth mailer is platform-operated. For a white-label or
enterprise customer that needs mail from its own domain, scope these items
explicitly:

- sender domain and DNS records;
- SPF, DKIM, DMARC, bounce, and complaint handling;
- whether MIOSA sends through a managed provider or the customer's private SMTP;
- per-tenant branding and template ownership;
- audit logs and delivery visibility;
- whether the setup is cloud, private-network, or on-prem.

Do not promise a dashboard toggle that lets each project configure its own auth sender.

## App-owned email

Generated apps can still send their own email by storing provider credentials
as project/runtime secrets and calling the provider directly from app code.
That is the right path for product emails such as receipts, invites, booking
confirmations, reports, or customer-specific notifications.

## Next

- [Project Auth](/docs/data/auth): Enable per-project signup, login, JWTs, password reset, and email confirmation.
- [Project integrations](/docs/integrations): Connect app-level services such as Stripe, Resend, Twilio, and webhooks.
- [Data overview](/docs/data/overview): Managed databases, storage, Redis, Qdrant, Auth, Volumes, and Fractal.
data/fractal:
MIOSA and Fractal run dedicated Fractal instances for massive-scale structured data and computation, secure and isolated for enterprise and government.

> **Caution: Enterprise engagement, not a self-service primitive**
>
> Fractal is not provisioned like Postgres, MySQL, Redis, Qdrant, Storage, Auth, or Volumes. A production Fractal instance is scoped as a MIOSA and Fractal enterprise engagement covering data residency, connector shape, credentials, sync, audit, approvals, and operating model.

---

## Who it is for

Fractal is for organizations whose data work is bigger than an application database:

- **Enterprise and government** teams that own client-wide structured data and cannot let AI near their systems of record.
- **Regulated industries**: electric, gas, and water utilities, telecommunications, financial services, healthcare, insurance, logistics, retail, oil and gas, and public sector.
- **Very large datasets**: millions of records, accounts, meters, claims, invoices, transactions, or assets.
- **High-volume computation** that is trivial per row and expensive once it runs millions of times a day.

If your data fits comfortably in a MIOSA Postgres database, you do not need Fractal. Use the built-in primitives and come back when the population, the calculation, or the isolation requirement outgrows them.

## What you get

- **Dedicated Fractal instances**: A Fractal instance dedicated to your data and workloads, separate from shared application databases and scoped to your organization.
- **Massive structured data**: Client-wide structured records and the high-volume calculations that are too large for the application database hot path.
- **Security and isolation**: A private data plane. AI reads and writes on the Fractal twin; your systems of record stay untouched.
- **Scaling**: Instances grow with the population and the job volume, for enterprise and government scale.
- **Reconciliation and audit**: Compare, score, and reconcile across source systems, with evidence and an auditable outcome for every run.
- **Deployment options**: Cloud, private, or government-oriented deployment, chosen to fit your residency and operating requirements.

## How it fits with MIOSA

MIOSA is the product and operating layer. Apps, agents, deployments, review queues, and audit trails connect to the Fractal data plane, so your customers see one branded product and never touch the data plumbing underneath.

- **MIOSA**: The product surface: apps, agents, sandboxes, computers, deployments, auth, review, approvals, audit, webhooks.
- **Fractal instance**: The enterprise data substrate: client-wide structured data, high-volume calculation, reconciliation, and a private data plane.
- **Customer systems**: Authoritative records, production write policy, residency requirements, and final source-system promotion.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Sources["Customer systems of record"] -->|one-way sync| Instance["Fractal instance"]
  Instance -->|datasets and findings| Surface["MIOSA product surface"]
  Surface -.->|approved promotion| Sources
```

Read it left to right:

1. Customer systems of record remain the source of truth, and data flows into the instance one way.
2. Fractal turns raw source data and business rules into an explicit enterprise model: ontology, taxonomy, and schema mapping.
3. The Fractal instance runs the heavy data work against that model: high-volume calculations, reconciliation, and derived datasets.
4. MIOSA turns those outputs into a product: apps, agents, deployments, review queues, approvals, reports, and audit trails.
5. Promotion back to source is controlled and approved. The agent proposes; customer policy decides what is promoted.

### The enterprise data model

The first job is not to point an agent at raw tables. The first job is to map the customer's world into a usable data model: the entities, relationships, names, identifiers, calculations, source-of-truth rules, and approval rules the business actually runs on.

| Model layer | Examples | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Ontology** | Customer, account, claim, invoice, meter | Names the real business objects |
| **Taxonomy** | Product families, claim types, rate classes | Groups data into business-safe categories |
| **Schema mapping** | Source fields, IDs, joins, units | Connects source systems to a stable model |
| **Calculation definitions** | Pricing, eligibility, reconciliation | Makes repeatable work explicit |
| **Governance rules** | Read-only and propose-only fields | Keeps agents from uncontrolled writes |

Business objects in a typical model include customer, account, claim, invoice, product, meter, asset, provider, and location. Taxonomy covers product families, claim types, customer segments, rate classes, regions, and exception categories. Governance rules mark fields read-only, propose-only, or approval-required for writeback, and set the audit requirements for each.

### Governed writeback

Fractal-backed workflows should not let AI write directly to production systems. Use a propose, review, promote shape:

```text
read scoped data
  -> run calculation or reconciliation
  -> produce finding or proposal with evidence
  -> route to human or policy approval
  -> promote through a controlled writeback service
  -> record audit outcome
```

### Connector expectations

Do not assume a public connector contract from this page. A production design is scoped with MIOSA and Fractal, and defines:

- dataset and tenant identity;
- data residency and network path;
- scoped credentials or token exchange;
- read-only, propose-only, and approval-required modes;
- sync health and freshness;
- audit and event handoff;
- writeback ownership and rollback or compensation policy.

## Fractal compared with MIOSA Postgres, Storage, and Volumes

Use the built-in primitives for normal application state. Reach for a Fractal instance when the population, the calculation, or the isolation requirement outgrows them.

| Need | MIOSA built-in | Fractal instance |
|---|---|---|
| App-local relational state | Postgres or MySQL | Not the right tool |
| Cache, queues, sessions | Redis | Not the right tool |
| Files, reports, exports | Object storage | Stores artifacts around Fractal runs |
| Durable disk for a sandbox | Volumes | Not the right tool |
| Embedding and vector search | Qdrant | Indexes Fractal outputs |
| End-user auth | Project Auth | Gates access before Fractal data |
| Client-wide structured data | Too large for the app DB | Dedicated Fractal instance |
| High-volume calculation | App code if small | Fractal-backed calculation |
| Reconciliation across sources | App code if small | Fractal-backed reconciliation |
| A private, isolated data plane | Not offered | Fractal instance in your environment |
| Keeping AI off systems of record | Not offered | Fractal digital twin, one-way sync |

## Deployment options

**Cloud**

A managed MIOSA product surface with a Fractal instance in the partner data plane. You get the branded app and the operating workflow; Fractal runs the enterprise data plane.

**Private**

The Fractal instance runs in your environment or private network, and production data never leaves your boundary. MIOSA connects to it from the product surface.

**Government**

Fractal publishes government-oriented material and a government contact path. Residency, network, and procurement requirements are scoped directly with MIOSA and Fractal.

A hybrid pilot is also common: prove the workflow on a restricted export or scoped dataset before any production promotion.

## Getting started

A Fractal-backed project starts as an enterprise architecture conversation, not a connector install. The usual sequence:

1. **Talk to us.** Describe the workflow, the systems of record, and the data that concerns you.
2. **Scope the data.** Decide what the instance sees, where it runs, and how data residency is handled.
3. **Map the model.** Define the ontology, taxonomy, and schema mapping the workflow needs.
4. **Choose the deployment** and the sync, freshness, and read, propose, and writeback modes.
5. **Build the product surface.** Apps, agents, review queues, reports, and audit trails around the Fractal instance.
6. **Prove it on real data.** Run a parallel pilot before promoting anything back to source.

> **Note: Plan an enterprise data architecture**
>
> For a MIOSA and Fractal engagement, contact [enterprise@miosa.ai](mailto:enterprise@miosa.ai). Use this when the customer needs private data-plane planning, on-prem or customer-controlled deployment, source-system mapping, ontology and taxonomy work, or governed writeback.

## FAQ

### Is Fractal a MIOSA primitive like Postgres?

No. Postgres, MySQL, Redis, Qdrant, Storage, Auth, and Volumes are self-service primitives you create from the platform. A Fractal instance is an enterprise engagement, scoped with MIOSA and Fractal.

### Does my data have to leave my environment?

No. A private deployment keeps the instance in your environment or private network. A cloud deployment puts the instance in the partner data plane instead.

### Can AI write to my production systems?

Not directly. Data flows into the instance one way, AI works on the twin, and results are promoted back to source only through a controlled, auditable process with explicit approval.

### What scale does this target?

Millions of records, accounts, meters, claims, invoices, transactions, or assets, and calculations repeated millions of times per day. Fractal states that its production deployments run at Fortune 500 scale across utilities, telecommunications, and financial services.

### Do you publish certifications?

This page does not list certifications. Government, defense, and regulated deployments are scoped directly with MIOSA and Fractal against your requirements.

### Is there a published performance or price figure?

Fractal publishes its own figures, including 100x performance, 90 percent less infrastructure cost, and a 90-day parallel deployment, on its public site. These are Fractal's claims, not MIOSA measurements. Treat them as a starting point for a pilot, not as a contract.

## Fractal's public claims and references

Fractal publishes the partner-side architecture as a synchronized digital twin, one-way synchronization from systems of record, controlled promotion back, locality optimization, commodity hardware, and industry-specific deployments. These are Fractal's own claims.

| Reference | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [Fractal](https://fractalweb.app/) | Digital twins, structured data, performance, and cost claims. |
| [How Fractal works](https://fractalweb.app/how) | Twin architecture, one-way sync, promoted results, 90-day pilot. |
| [Why Fractal](https://fractalweb.app/why) | Corruption risk, what does not work, and the cost case. |
| [Markets](https://fractalweb.app/markets) | Utilities, telecom, finance, healthcare, insurance, government. |
| [About](https://fractalweb.app/about) | Origins, locality optimization, production deployments. |
| [Contact](https://fractalweb.app/contact) | Fractal's own intake and scheduling flow. |

## Common enterprise workflows

| Workflow | MIOSA role | Fractal role |
|---|---|---|
| Billing QA | App, review, approvals, audit | Calculation and mismatch detection |
| Claims or revenue reconciliation | Agents, evidence UI, artifacts | Reconciliation across records |
| Product variant analysis | Workflow UI, result publishing | High-volume variant calculation |
| Agent execution evaluation | Orchestration, reports, review | Structured execution outputs |
| Customer data operations | White-label product, webhooks | Client-wide structured data plane |

data/mongodb:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Managed MongoDB is a database engine like Postgres, MySQL and Redis.
> It runs the official MongoDB 7 server in its own microVM with a persistent data volume.

## What you get

A managed MongoDB 7 instance with an auto-generated root user and password, injected as `MONGODB_URI` (also `MONGO_URL`):

```bash
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://user:pass@host:port/miosa_db?authSource=admin
```

Standard MongoDB drivers work without modification:

```typescript
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb"
const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI!)
await client.connect()

const users = client.db("miosa_db").collection("users")
await users.insertOne({ name: "Ada", createdAt: new Date() })
```

The user has the root role, so you can create any number of databases on the instance.
`authSource=admin` is part of the URL and must stay.

## Provision

```bash
miosa db create --name app-mongo --engine mongodb
```

```typescript
await miosa.databases.create({ name: "app-mongo", engine: "mongodb", size: "small" })
```

You can also choose MongoDB in the Add menu of a project, or set `managed: mongodb` on a database service in a change set.
Only major version 7 is available.

## Connection variables

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `MONGODB_URI` | Full connection string |
| `MONGO_URL` | Same as `MONGODB_URI` |
| `MONGO_HOST`, `MONGO_PORT` | Host and port |
| `MONGO_USER`, `MONGO_PASSWORD` | Root user and password |
| `MONGO_DATABASE` | Default database name |

## Backups and restore

Backups are logical (`mongodump`, gzip archive) and cover every database on the instance except `admin` and `config`.
A restore replaces the collections the backup contains and leaves the others alone.
It never touches the `admin` database, so your issued credentials keep working.
A MongoDB backup restores only into a MongoDB database.

## Limits

- There is no table browser or query console for MongoDB. Use `mongosh` or a driver.
- There is no automatic pause when idle, as with MySQL and Redis.
- Memory, connections and storage follow the selected plan size.

## See also

- [Overview](/docs/data/overview)
- [Redis](/docs/data/redis)
- [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres)
data/mysql:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Managed MySQL is available for projects that need MySQL-compatible schemas,
> frameworks, or imports. MIOSA provisions the instance, stores credentials, and
> injects `DATABASE_URL` into attached sandboxes and production runtimes.

## When to use MySQL

Use managed MySQL when the application already expects MySQL semantics:

- Laravel, WordPress, or MySQL-first frameworks
- Existing customer schemas that should not be converted to Postgres
- SQL workloads that rely on MySQL-specific behavior
- SaaS templates that ship with MySQL migrations

Use [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres) when you need richer relational features,
extensions, or Postgres-native tooling.

## Runtime contract

Applications do not need to know where the database runs. Read the injected
connection string at boot:

```bash
DATABASE_URL=mysql://user:password@host:3306/database
```

MIOSA injects the same variable into:

- sandboxes for development and agent work
- runtime instances for production deployments
- background workers that belong to the project

Lifecycle, backup, restore, credentials, logs, and metrics use the common [Databases API](/docs/api-reference/databases).
Do not infer those values from a hostname or project slug.

## Provisioning pattern

```typescript
const project = await miosa.projects.create({
  name: "Customer Portal",
  data: { mysql: true },
});
```

For app builders and white-label platforms, create MySQL per customer project
when the generated app requires it. Keep schema migrations in the application
repo or sandbox workspace so deployments remain repeatable.

## See also

- [Data overview](/docs/data/overview): Choose the right data service for each workload.
- [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres): Managed relational database for Postgres-native applications.
- [Environments](/docs/docker-host/environments): Separate production, staging, and development credentials.

MIOSA Data services give your sandboxes and production runtime instances access to persistent storage without any external account setup. When you attach a data service to a project, MIOSA provisions the resource and injects its credentials at boot - your code reads `process.env.DATABASE_URL` and connects. Pick the right one for your data shape: | Service | Use when you need | Persistence | |---|---|---| | **Postgres** | Relational data, joins, transactions, migrations | Durable - survives deploys and sandbox destruction | | **MySQL** | MySQL-compatible apps, existing MySQL schemas | Durable - survives deploys and sandbox destruction | | **Redis** | Cache, sessions, pub/sub, rate limiting | Durable (AOF/RDB) but treated as cache-class | | **MongoDB** | Document data, flexible schemas | Durable - survives deploys and sandbox destruction | | **Qdrant** | Vector search, semantic similarity, embeddings | Durable - collection data persists across VMs | | **Storage** | File uploads, generated assets, binary blobs | Durable - content-addressed object store | | **Auth** | Per-project end-user signup, login, and JWT issuance | Durable - user records outlive any VM | | **Volumes** | Large or fast filesystem state that does not fit in Postgres | Attached to one runtime instance at a time | ## Data persists past your VMs Sandboxes are persistent by default and can be paused, resumed, snapshotted, or destroyed. Deployment runtime instances are replaceable. Managed data has an independent lifecycle and is not deleted when either compute surface is replaced. Destroying a sandbox removes the VM - the connected Postgres database is untouched. Publishing a new version does not migrate your schema. Rolling back a deployment does not roll back your database. Data services are managed independently of the compute that connects to them. This is intentional. It is also why production stays available during deploys: the new version connects to the same database the old version was using. ## How credentials are injected MIOSA can bind different database credentials to different deployment environments: ```text production runtime → DATABASE_URL = postgres://prod-db... staging runtime → DATABASE_URL = postgres://staging-db... ``` You ship one environment variable name and MIOSA resolves the binding for that environment. ## Provision

When a project is created with `data: { postgres: true }`, MIOSA provisions a logical database in a managed Postgres cluster, generates credentials, and injects them as env vars.

```mermaid
graph LR
    PC[Project create] -->|data.postgres=true| MP[MIOSA provisioner]
    MP --> PG[(Managed Postgres cluster)]
    PG -->|credentials generated| ENV[DATABASE_URL env var]
    ENV --> SB[Sandbox]
    ENV --> RI[Runtime Instance]
```
```typescript
const project = await miosa.projects.create({
  name: "Team Portal",
  data: { postgres: true },
})

// Sandboxes and runtime instances under this project boot with:
// DATABASE_URL = postgresql://user:pass@host:port/proj_xxx
```

You can also add Postgres to an existing project:
```typescript
await miosa.projects.dataServices.create(projectId, {
  type: "postgres",
  size: "small",  // small | medium | large
})
```

## Create it your way: API, CLI, or SDK

You don't need an SDK. The same managed database can be created and used three ways. All of these hit the same API.

**Raw API (curl):**
```bash
# 1. Create a Postgres database
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/databases \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "my-db", "engine": "postgresql"}'
# → { "id": "db_...", "state": "provisioning", ... }   (reaches "running" in ~30-60s)

# 2. Get the connection string once it's running
curl https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/databases/DB_ID/credentials \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
# → { "data": { "recommended_url": "postgresql://user:pass@host:port/miosa_db", ... } }

# 3. Connect with anything that speaks Postgres
psql "postgresql://user:pass@host:port/miosa_db"
```
Other engines: pass `"engine": "mysql"`, `"redis"`, or `"qdrant"`.

**CLI:**
```bash
miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name": "my-db", "engine": "postgresql"}'  # create
miosa db list                     # see them + their state
miosa db connection <id>                    # open a shell to it
miosa db logs <id>                       # tail logs
miosa db backup <id>                     # snapshot
miosa api POST /databases/<id>/restore \
  -d '{"backup_id": "<backup-id>"}'          # restore
```

**SDK** (Python example below; TypeScript/Go/Elixir SDKs have the same methods).

## Connection management

Use a bounded application connection pool and size it for the database plan.
Treat the connection URL returned by the credentials endpoint as authoritative.
Do not assume a separate session or transaction pooler unless the returned database configuration explicitly advertises one.

## Where you can connect from

The connection URL points at a private MIOSA address.
It is reachable from sandboxes, computers and deployments in your organization.
It is not reachable from the public internet, so `psql` on your laptop cannot use it directly.
To work with the database from your own machine, run `psql` inside a sandbox, or open a tunnel through one.

## Schema management is yours

MIOSA doesn't run migrations for you. The recommended workflow:

1. Use your framework's migration tool (Prisma, Drizzle, Ecto, Alembic, etc.).
2. Run migrations as part of your build or startup, or as a separate one-off:

```typescript
await sandbox.exec({ cmd: "npx", args: ["prisma", "migrate", "deploy"] })
```

3. Make migrations backward-compatible (expand → migrate → contract). This keeps rollback working  -  see [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback).

## Owner privileges

The user in your connection URL is the database's owner role.
By default it owns the database and everything it creates, and nothing more: it cannot create roles or databases, and row-level security applies to it.

Some migrations need more.
Migrations written for Supabase or Railway often create their own roles, grant to a role named `postgres`, run `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres`, or rely on the owner reading past row-level security.
For those, turn on the **elevated** owner:

| | Standard (default) | Elevated |
|---|---|---|
| Owns the database and its objects | Yes | Yes |
| `CREATEROLE` (create and grant your own roles) | No | Yes |
| `CREATEDB` | No | Yes |
| `BYPASSRLS` (reads past row-level security) | No | Yes |
| Member of a `NOLOGIN` role named `postgres` | No | Yes |
| Superuser | No | No |

The elevated owner is never a superuser.
`COPY ... TO PROGRAM`, untrusted languages such as `plpython3u`, `pg_read_server_files`, `ALTER SYSTEM` and extensions outside the [allowed list](/docs/data/postgres#extensions) stay refused.
A migration that changes the `SUPERUSER` attribute, for example `ALTER ROLE app NOSUPERUSER`, still fails: remove that clause, since roles you create are not superusers anyway.

It is available on PostgreSQL 16 or later, on paid plans (Developer and up), and is off unless you turn it on for a database.

**Turn it on when you create the database:**

```bash
miosa db create app-db --version 16 --owner-privileges elevated
```

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/databases \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "app-db", "engine": "postgresql", "owner_privileges": true}'
```

**Or change an existing database:**

```bash
miosa db update app-db --owner-privileges elevated
miosa db update app-db --owner-privileges standard
```

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/databases/DB_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"owner_privileges": true}'
```

On a running database the change is applied before the request returns.
On a stopped database it is saved and applied the next time the database starts.
`miosa db get app-db` and the API's `owner_privileges` field show the current setting.

Returning to standard removes the attributes and the `postgres` membership again.
It does not drop roles or databases created while the owner was elevated: drop those yourself if you no longer want them.
Every change made from your organization is recorded in its audit log as `database.owner_privileges.enabled` or `database.owner_privileges.disabled`, with the member or API key that made it.

> **Caution: Who can use it**
>
> Anyone with the owner's connection URL gets these privileges: they can create roles that can sign in, and read rows that row-level security would hide.
> Give your application a separate, less privileged role if it does not need them.

## Extensions

These extensions can be used in a database: `vector`, `pg_trgm`, `pgcrypto`, `uuid-ossp`, `citext`, `hstore`, `btree_gin`, `btree_gist` and `pg_stat_statements`. Ask for the ones you want when you create the database:

```bash
miosa db create app-db --extensions vector,pg_trgm
```

Anything else (for example `adminpack` or `file_fdw`) is refused.

### pg_stat_statements is on by default

Every **new** Postgres database has `pg_stat_statements` turned on, so the console's top-queries view and your own `SELECT ... FROM pg_stat_statements` work from the first minute. It is added to the list you ask for, and `pg_stat_statements.track` is the Postgres default (`top`).

To create a database without it, send `"pg_stat_statements": false` when you create it:

```bash
miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-db","engine":"postgres","pg_stat_statements":false}'
```

Databases that already exist are not changed. To turn it on for one of them, enable the extension on that database; it takes effect the next time you restart it.

## Backups

MIOSA supports scheduled backups and on-demand backups stored outside the database runtime.
Retention depends on the database plan.

Create an on-demand backup:

```bash
miosa db backup <database-id> --json
```

Restore from a selected backup:

```bash
miosa api POST /databases/<database-id>/restore \
  -d '{"backup_id": "<backup-id>"}'
```

Restore replaces database contents.
Review the target database and backup ID before confirming the operation.

## Lifecycle and recovery

create creates provisioning; provisioning goes to running on ready; running goes to stopped on stop, and back to running on start.

running goes to restarting on restart or maintenance; restarting goes to running on verified.

restarting goes to error on recovery fails.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provisioning` | MIOSA is creating storage, credentials, and the database runtime. |
| `running` | The database accepts connections. |
| `stopped` | The database was intentionally stopped. Persistent data remains attached. |
| `restarting` | MIOSA is restoring the desired-running database after maintenance or a restart request. |
| `error` | Recovery did not complete and operator action is required. |

During host maintenance, MIOSA preserves the database ID, credentials, persistent volume, bindings, and desired state.
A database that was running is restarted and verified before its host returns to active service.
An intentionally stopped database remains stopped.

## Sandboxed development with the same DB

When you create a sandbox under a project that has Postgres, the sandbox also gets `DATABASE_URL`  -  pointing at the same managed database. Two options:

1. **Shared dev DB.** Sandboxes and production both point at the production database. Fast iteration, risk of dev work affecting prod data.
2. **Per-environment DB.** Production gets one DB, staging/dev get another. Configured via [Environments](/docs/docker-host/environments).

Default is (2) once per-environment isolation lands. Until then, sandboxes share the production DB; use schema namespacing or be careful with destructive queries.

## Connecting from a sandbox
```typescript
await sandbox.exec({
  cmd: "psql",
  args: [process.env.DATABASE_URL, "-c", "SELECT 1"],
})
```

The sandbox's `DATABASE_URL` is the same shape the runtime would see in production. Whatever code works in the sandbox works in the deployment.

## Limits

| Tier | Storage | Connections (PgBouncer) | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| small | 1 GB | 100 | 512 MB |
| medium | 10 GB | 200 | 2 GB |
| large | 100 GB | 500 | 8 GB |

Storage, connection, and memory limits depend on the database plan.
Inspect the database response and metrics rather than assuming automatic storage growth.

## Costs

Postgres pricing is in two parts:

- **Compute**  -  per-hour while the DB is running (always-on by default for production; can be paused for sandboxed dev DBs).
- **Storage**  -  GB-month for data plus WAL.

See [Usage & Billing](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing). Per-database metering carries [attribution](/docs/platform/attribution), so platforms can charge back per end-customer.

## Bring your own Postgres?

If you'd rather use an external Postgres, just set `DATABASE_URL` as an env var on the deployment and skip the managed offering:
```typescript
await miosa.deployments.env.set(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
  vars: { DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://...your-external-db..." },
})
```

MIOSA's runtime injects whatever you set. The managed Postgres is convenience; bringing your own is supported.

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# Provision a managed database
db = miosa.databases.create(
    name="team-portal-db",
    engine="postgres",
    size="small",
```

data/public-endpoint:
A managed database is reachable from inside the platform by its private URL. Turn
on public networking when something outside needs to connect: a laptop, a
migration tool, an analytics job in another cloud.

```bash
miosa db public app-db                       # off or on, and the address
miosa db public app-db on                    # any source
miosa db public app-db on --allow 203.0.113.0/24 --allow 198.51.100.7
miosa db public app-db off                  # close it and free the port
```

The same calls are `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE /api/v1/databases/:id/public-networking`.

## What you get

- A host and a port from **30000-39999**, one port per database. The host is the
  edge's public address, so it does not change when the database moves host.
- `public_url` in the credentials response while it is on, and
  `DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL` in the database service's variables, so
  `${{db.DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL}}` resolves for anything that needs it.

## Security

- **TLS only.** Postgres needs `sslmode=require`; MySQL needs
  `--ssl-mode=REQUIRED` and refuses a plaintext login with error 3159. The
  certificate is self-signed, so `require` encrypts without verifying the name.
- **The allowlist closes disallowed sources before any TLS handshake.** `--allow`
  replaces the stored list, so `on` with no `--allow` means any source. Entries
  are IPs or CIDRs, at most 32.
- Limits: 100 connections per database, 20 new connections per 10 seconds per
  source IP, at most 32 TLS handshakes at once, and 2,000 public connections
  across your databases.

## Engines

Postgres, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB. Other engines answer `ENGINE_NOT_SUPPORTED`.

## Turning it off

`off`, or deleting the database, closes the port within about fifteen seconds.
Both are recorded in the audit log as `database.public_networking_enable` and
`database.public_networking_disable`.

> **Note: Prefer the private URL**
>
> Anything inside the platform should use the private URL. The public endpoint
> exists for clients that cannot reach the private network, not as the default way
> to connect.

## When to use Qdrant

Use Qdrant when an agent or app needs durable semantic memory:

- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
- Document and knowledge-base search
- Product or lead similarity matching
- Long-running agent memory across sessions
- Embeddings produced inside sandboxes or computers

Use object storage for the raw files and Qdrant for the vectors and payload metadata that make those files searchable.

## What you get

Per project: a dedicated Qdrant instance. Credentials injected at boot:

```bash
QDRANT_URL=https://qdrant.proj_xxx.miosa.internal
QDRANT_API_KEY=...
```

Use any Qdrant-compatible client:

```typescript
import { QdrantClient } from "@qdrant/js-client-rest"

const client = new QdrantClient({
  url: process.env.QDRANT_URL,
  apiKey: process.env.QDRANT_API_KEY,
})

// Create a collection
await client.createCollection("documents", {
  vectors: { size: 1536, distance: "Cosine" },
})

// Upsert vectors
await client.upsert("documents", {
  points: [
    { id: 1, vector: embedding, payload: { text: "Hello world" } },
  ],
})

// Semantic search
const results = await client.search("documents", {
  vector: queryEmbedding,
  limit: 5,
  with_payload: true,
})
```

```python
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
import os

client = QdrantClient(
    url=os.environ["QDRANT_URL"],
    api_key=os.environ["QDRANT_API_KEY"],
)

results = client.search(
    collection_name="documents",
    query_vector=query_embedding,
    limit=5,
)
```

```typescript
const project = await miosa.projects.create({
  name: "my-rag-app",
  data: { qdrant: true },
})
```

Or add to an existing project:

```typescript
await miosa.projects.dataServices.create(projectId, {
  type: "qdrant",
  size: "small",  // small | medium | large
})
```

**cURL:**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/data-services \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
```

## Data persists past VM destroy

Collections and vectors survive sandbox destruction and deployment rollbacks. The Qdrant instance keeps running between VM lifecycles. You do not need to re-index on every boot.

## Typical pattern: RAG pipeline

```typescript
import OpenAI from "openai"
import { QdrantClient } from "@qdrant/js-client-rest"

const openai = new OpenAI()
const qdrant = new QdrantClient({
  url: process.env.QDRANT_URL,
  apiKey: process.env.QDRANT_API_KEY,
})

// Index a document
async function index(id: number, text: string) {
  const { data } = await openai.embeddings.create({
    model: "text-embedding-3-small",
    input: text,
  })
  await qdrant.upsert("docs", {
    points: [{ id, vector: data[0].embedding, payload: { text } }],
  })
}

// Query
async function query(question: string, topK = 5) {
  const { data } = await openai.embeddings.create({
    model: "text-embedding-3-small",
    input: question,
  })
  return qdrant.search("docs", {
    vector: data[0].embedding,
    limit: topK,
    with_payload: true,
  })
}
```

## Limits

| Tier | Memory | Disk | Max collections |
|---|---|---|---|
| small | 1 GB | 10 GB | 10 |
| medium | 4 GB | 50 GB | 50 |
| large | 16 GB | 200 GB | unlimited |

Vector count per collection is bounded by memory. At 1536 dimensions (OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small`), `small` fits ~100K vectors; `medium` fits ~400K.

Yes. Set `QDRANT_URL` and `QDRANT_API_KEY` as env vars to point at an external instance (Qdrant Cloud, self-hosted):

```typescript
await miosa.deployments.env.set(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
  vars: {
    QDRANT_URL: "https://your-cluster.qdrant.io",
    QDRANT_API_KEY: "your-api-key",
  },
})
```

```python
print(creds["url"])       # https://qdrant.proj_xxx.miosa.internal
print(creds["api_key"])

# Teardown
miosa.databases.delete(qdrant["id"])
```

data/redis:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Managed Redis is live.
> Per-project instances and `REDIS_URL` injection are available.
> Redis is provisioned or attached explicitly and should not be assumed to exist in every sandbox template.

## What you get

Per project: a managed Redis instance, with credentials injected as `REDIS_URL`:
```bash

REDIS_URL=redis://default:pass@host:port/0
```

Standard Redis clients work without modification:
```typescript
import { createClient } from "redis"
const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL })
await redis.connect()

await redis.set("user:123:last-seen", new Date().toISOString())
const value = await redis.get("user:123:last-seen")
```

## Use cases

- **Cache**  -  short-lived computed results.
- **Sessions**  -  express-session / Phoenix sessions / similar.
- **Pub/sub**  -  agent coordination, real-time fan-out.
- **Rate limiting**  -  atomic INCR + TTL.
- **Job queues**  -  Bull, BullMQ, Sidekiq, Oban-light alternatives.

For full job-queue workloads at scale, MIOSA has a [Background Jobs](/docs/docker-host/runtime-instances) primitive that's a better fit than rolling your own on Redis.

## Provision
```typescript
await miosa.projects.dataServices.create(projectId, {
  type: "redis",
  size: "small",  // small | medium | large
})
```

## Limits and durability

Memory, connection, and persistence settings depend on the returned managed-database plan.
Inspect the database response and metrics for the selected instance.
Treat Redis as cache-class unless the selected plan explicitly guarantees the durability required by your application.

## Pub/sub considerations

If you're using Redis pub/sub for cross-runtime coordination, multiple runtime instances of the same service can all subscribe  -  MIOSA does not deduplicate or proxy pub/sub. For higher-volume real-time fan-out, consider SSE through MIOSA's [Events](/docs/api-reference/events) or a dedicated message broker.

## Bring your own Redis?

Yes. Set `REDIS_URL` as an env var to whatever external Redis you prefer (Upstash, AWS ElastiCache, your own).

## See also

- [Overview](/docs/data/overview)  -  the broader data plane
- [Runtime Instances](/docs/docker-host/runtime-instances)  -  for background-job workloads
data/storage:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Object storage is shipped. Buckets, objects, presigned URL (upload and download), quota enforcement, and per-tenant isolation are all live. Large direct uploads (>5 MB) should use the presigned path; see the limits table below.

## What you get

Per project: an S3-compatible bucket, accessed through MIOSA endpoints. Credentials injected as env vars:
```bash

STORAGE_BUCKET=miosa-proj_xxx-uploads
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=https://storage.miosa.app
STORAGE_KEY_ID=...
STORAGE_KEY_SECRET=...
```

Your code uses the standard S3 client libraries:
```typescript
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3"

const s3 = new S3Client({
  endpoint: process.env.STORAGE_ENDPOINT,
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: process.env.STORAGE_KEY_ID!,
    secretAccessKey: process.env.STORAGE_KEY_SECRET!,
  },
  region: "us-east-1",
})

await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
  Bucket: process.env.STORAGE_BUCKET,
  Key: "uploads/foo.png",
  Body: pngBuffer,
}))
```

## Use it your way: API, CLI, or SDK

No SDK required. Same bucket, three ways.

> Storage calls need an API key with the `storage:read` / `storage:write` scope. Mint one with `POST /api/v1/api-keys {"scopes": ["storage:read","storage:write"]}`. A plain key gets a 403 telling you which scope is missing.

**Raw API (curl):**
```bash
# Create a bucket
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/storage/buckets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "my-bucket"}'

# Upload an object (binary → application/octet-stream)
curl -X PUT "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/storage/buckets/BUCKET_ID/objects/path/file.txt" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" --data-binary @file.txt

# Download it
curl "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/storage/buckets/BUCKET_ID/objects/path/file.txt" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

# Presign a URL so a browser can upload/download directly (no proxy)
curl -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/storage/buckets/BUCKET_ID/presign" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"key": "path/file.txt", "method": "GET"}'
```

**CLI:**
```bash
miosa storage create my-bucket
miosa storage list
miosa storage objects <bucket-id>
```

Upload, download and presigning have no dedicated subcommand; drive them with `miosa api`:

```bash
# Upload an object
miosa api PUT /storage/buckets/<bucket-id>/objects/path/file.txt \
  -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" -d @./file.txt

# Download it
miosa api GET /storage/buckets/<bucket-id>/objects/path/file.txt

# Presign a URL so a browser can upload/download directly (no proxy)
miosa api POST /storage/buckets/<bucket-id>/presign \
  -d '{"key": "path/file.txt", "method": "GET"}'
```

## Signed URLs for browser uploads

Don't proxy file uploads through your runtime. Mint a signed URL server-side; the browser uploads directly to storage:
```typescript
// Server
const url = await miosa.storage.signedUrl({
  bucket: process.env.STORAGE_BUCKET!,
  key: `users/${userId}/avatar.png`,
  operation: "put",
  expiresInSec: 300,
  contentType: "image/png",
})
return { uploadUrl: url }
```
```typescript
// Browser
await fetch(uploadUrl, {
  method: "PUT",
  body: file,
  headers: { "Content-Type": "image/png" },
})
```

Same pattern for downloads (`operation: "get"`). Signed URLs are scoped (single key, single operation, short expiry)  -  no risk of leaking bucket-wide credentials to a browser.

## Public vs private

Each object can be private (default; access only via signed URL) or public (served from a `*.storage.miosa.app` URL). Public objects can also be fronted by a custom domain via your project's [Domain](/docs/docker-host/domains) settings.

## Bandwidth and storage costs

Two billable dimensions:

- **Storage**  -  GB-month for stored bytes.
- **Egress**  -  GB out from MIOSA to the public internet. Storage-to-runtime within MIOSA is free.

[Attribution](/docs/platform/attribution) is carried on every event for chargeback.

## Limits

| Limit | Default | Tunable |
|---|---|---|
| Storage per project | 1 GB | Yes (plan-dependent) |
| Direct API upload size | 5 MB verified | Larger uploads should use presigned/direct storage |
| Max object size | 5 GB target | Up to 100 GB target for multipart |
| List keys per call | 1000 | Standard S3 pagination |

> **Note**
>
> The latest live storage smoke on June 9, 2026 verified create, upload,
> download, SHA-256 validation, and cleanup through `10 / 10` sequential `5 MB`
> objects. `8 MB` and `10 MB` direct raw uploads currently fail before storage, so
> large files should use presigned URLs or S3-compatible direct upload flows until
> the streaming API path is promoted. See [Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks) for the
> measured table and the ComputeSDK storage comparison.

## Sandboxes can use the bucket too

The same env vars are injected into sandboxes for dev / testing. Upload from inside a sandbox:
```typescript
await sandbox.exec({
  cmd: "aws",
  args: ["s3", "cp", "/workspace/build.tar.gz", `s3://${process.env.STORAGE_BUCKET}/builds/`],
  env: {
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: process.env.STORAGE_KEY_ID,
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: process.env.STORAGE_KEY_SECRET,
    AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: process.env.STORAGE_ENDPOINT,
  },
})
```

## Bring your own bucket?

Yes. Set the env vars to point at an external S3-compatible bucket (real AWS, Backblaze B2, R2, etc.). MIOSA injects whatever you set.

## Python SDK

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# Create a bucket
bucket = miosa.storage.create_bucket("my-uploads", public=False)
bucket_id = bucket["id"]

# Upload bytes
with open("report.pdf", "rb") as f:
    miosa.storage.put_object(bucket_id, "reports/report.pdf", f.read(),
                             content_type="application/pdf")

# Mint a presigned URL for browser upload (PUT)
presigned = miosa.storage.presign(
    bucket_id,
    key="avatars/user-123.png",
    operation="put",
    expires_in_sec=300,
    content_type="image/png",
)
print(presigned["url"])

# Mint a presigned URL for browser download (GET)
download = miosa.storage.presign(
    bucket_id,
    key="reports/report.pdf",
    operation="get",
    expires_in_sec=3600,
)
print(download["url"])

# List objects with a prefix
objects = miosa.storage.list_objects(bucket_id, prefix="reports/")
for obj in objects:
    print(obj["key"], obj["size"])

# Delete a bucket
miosa.storage.delete_bucket(bucket_id)
```

data/volumes:
> **Tip: Available**
>
> Volumes are live.
> Create a persistent block device, attach it to a compatible computer on the same host, and preserve writes independently of the computer lifecycle.
> Attachment to a replacement computer is explicit.
> Most workloads should use [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres) or [Storage](/docs/data/storage) because local volumes are host-bound.

A **Volume** is a persistent block device attached to a compatible computer.
It survives ordinary computer restarts while the host-local volume remains healthy.
It does not automatically move across hosts.
Useful cases include:

- SQLite databases that need to be local to the runtime.
- Caches you can't afford to lose on restart.
- LLM model weights downloaded once and shared across instances.
- Workloads that legitimately need filesystem state (not just key-value).

Volumes are NOT useful for:

- Stateful databases  -  use [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres) instead. It scales better, backs up automatically, and survives host failures.
- User-uploaded files  -  use [Storage / Buckets](/docs/data/storage). Cheaper, browser-uploadable, geo-replicable.
- Shared state across multiple replicas  -  volumes are typically attached to ONE runtime instance.

## Create

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await miosa.projects.dataServices.create(projectId, {
  type: "volume",
  name: "model-weights",
  sizeGb: 50,
})
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# Create a 50 GB volume
vol = miosa.volumes.create(name="model-weights", size_gb=50)
print(vol["id"])  # vol_...

# List all volumes
for v in miosa.volumes.list():
    print(v["name"], v["size_gb"], "GB")

# Delete a volume
miosa.volumes.delete(vol["id"])
```

## Use it your way: API, CLI, or SDK

No SDK required.

**Raw API (curl):** the raw API takes `size_bytes` and a `backend` (use `local`).
```bash
# Create a 50 GB volume
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/volumes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "model-weights", "size_bytes": 53687091200, "backend": "local"}'

# Attach it to a running computer at a mount path
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/computers/COMPUTER_ID/volumes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"volume_id": "VOL_ID", "mount_path": "/mnt/data"}'

# Detach (by attachment id)
curl -X DELETE https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/computers/COMPUTER_ID/volumes/ATTACHMENT_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

**CLI:**
```bash
miosa volume create model-weights --size-gb 50
miosa volume list
```

Attach and detach are per-computer; drive them with `miosa api`:

```bash
# Attach the volume to a running computer at a mount path
miosa api POST /computers/<computer-id>/volumes \
  -d '{"volume_id": "<volume-id>", "mount_path": "/mnt/data"}'

# Detach by attachment id
miosa api DELETE /computers/<computer-id>/volumes/<attachment-id>
```

Delete a volume (it must be detached first):

```bash
miosa volume rm <volume-id>
```

> A local-backend volume lives on one host, so it attaches to computers on that same host. Cross-host attach returns a clear error rather than failing silently.

## Mount

A volume is mounted into the runtime instance's filesystem at a path:
```typescript
await miosa.services.update(serviceId, {
  volumes: [
    { dataServiceId: volumeId, mountPath: "/var/models" },
  ],
})
```

At boot, `/var/models` is the volume's contents. Writes persist.

## Replicas and volumes

Most volumes attach to a single runtime instance. If you scale a service to N replicas, by default each replica gets the **same volume mount** if it's marked `shared: true`, or its own volume if `shared: false`.

Shared volumes have all the usual concurrency caveats (filesystem locks, file-corruption risk if multiple writers touch the same file). Use Postgres for shared state unless you really know what you're doing.

## Limits

| Limit | Default |
|---|---|
| Max volume size | 500 GB |
| Max volumes per project | 10 |
| Filesystem | ext4 |
| Host placement | Must match the computer host |

## When to use a volume

Realistic short list:

1. You're shipping a self-hosted SQLite-backed app to keep deployment simple.
2. You're running an LLM inference service and don't want to re-download model weights on every instance start.
3. You have a writable filesystem cache that's expensive to rebuild.

Anything else, use Postgres or Storage.
